Problem.description: Problem Investigation #1: Investigating systemic underlying root cause for repeated incident alerts on db-postgres-primary.
Problem.rootCause: Unindexed database query performing full table scan during nightly backup batch.
Problem.workaround: Restart connection pool proxy service and scale max connections from 200 to 500.

Problem.shortDescription: Active Directory Kerberos Ticket Expiration Sync Failure (#2)
Problem.description: Problem Investigation #2: Investigating systemic underlying root cause for repeated incident alerts on k8s-prod-cluster-east-1.
Problem.rootCause: Clock skew drift between Active Directory DC 01 and NTP server exceeds 300 seconds.
Problem.workaround: Purge expired KBT cache on primary domain controller host dc-east-01.

Problem.shortDescription: Kubernetes Ingress NGINX Memory Leak under High Traffic Load (#3)
Problem.description: Problem Investigation #3: Investigating systemic underlying root cause for repeated incident alerts on ad-dc-master-01.
Problem.rootCause: Memory buffer leak in NGINX v1.21 ingress worker process during HTTP/2 multiplexing.
Problem.workaround: Trigger pod rolling restart and increase pod memory limits from 2Gi to 8Gi.

Problem.shortDescription: Okta Webhook Session Token Timeout on SSO Portal (#4)
Problem.description: Problem Investigation #4: Investigating systemic underlying root cause for repeated incident alerts on okta-auth-gw-01.
Problem.rootCause: OAuth callback handler missing retry backoff header handling under rate-limiting.
Problem.workaround: Force OAuth 2.0 token re-issuance and clear Redis session key cache.

Problem.shortDescription: SAP Financials ERP Database Deadlock during End-of-Month Run (#5)
Problem.description: Problem Investigation #5: Investigating systemic underlying root cause for repeated incident alerts on control plane.
Problem.rootCause: BGP route flapping caused by faulty fiber SFP transceiver on interface eth0.
Problem.workaround: Execute `sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1` and flush BGP neighbor tables.

KnowledgeArticle.title: Master SOP: Linux User Account Creation & Access Provisioning (Single or Bulk, Admin / Restricted / Standard Access)
KnowledgeArticle.content:
Master SOP: Linux User Account Provisioning & Sudo Access Runbook

OVERVIEW:
This Master SOP governs creating Linux user accounts (e.g. Pamsudo1 to Pamsudo5, User01 to User20) on WorkerNode1HL and configuring /etc/sudoers.d/ entry files to grant targeted execution rights (e.g. su - jboss, systemctl commands).

PROCEDURES:
1. Create user accounts (Pamsudo1..Pamsudo5):
   ssh root@192.168.100.101 "for u in Pamsudo1 Pamsudo2 Pamsudo3 Pamsudo4 Pamsudo5; do useradd -m -s /bin/bash $u 2>/dev/null || true; done"

2. Configure /etc/sudoers.d/ permissions:
   ssh root@192.168.100.101 "for u in Pamsudo1 Pamsudo2 Pamsudo3 Pamsudo4 Pamsudo5; do echo "$u ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /bin/su - jboss" > /etc/sudoers.d/$u && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/$u; done && visudo -c"
KnowledgeArticle.summary: One reusable SOP for provisioning Linux user accounts, covering every combination the ticket may ask for: a single user or a batch of many users, and full admin (passwordless sudo), restricted single-command sudo, or a standard account with no sudo at all. Read the step labels and pick only the block(s) that match what the ticket actually requests.
symptoms: Create a new Linux user account
Provision a user with admin/root/full sudo access
Grant a user restricted sudo access to run one specific command
Create a standard user with no elevated privileges
Bulk-create multiple Linux user accounts in one request
KnowledgeArticle.rootCause: Consolidated from 9 near-duplicate KB articles (KB0000006, KB0000016, KB0000027-30, KB0000036-37, KB0468213) that each hardcoded one specific scenario. The dynamic ReAct execution loop reads the labeled step blocks and, per its command-adaptation rules, selects and parameterizes only the block(s) matching the ticket's actual requirements (quantity and access level) rather than needing a separate KB per combination.
resolutionSteps: [VERIFY] id -u {username} &>/dev/null && echo 'User already exists' || echo 'User does not exist, proceeding'
[CREATE - BULK USERS] for u in {username_list}; do id -u "$u" &>/dev/null || useradd -m -s /bin/bash "$u"; done
[SET PASSWORD - only if the ticket provides one] echo '{username}:{password}' | chpasswd

[ACCESS: FULL ADMIN — use only when the ticket says 'admin access', 'root access', or 'full sudo'] echo '{username} ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/99-{username} && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/99-{username} && visudo -c -f /etc/sudoers.d/99-{username}

[ACCESS: FULL ADMIN, BULK — same as above but for every user in the batch] for u in {username_list}; do echo "$u ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL" > "/etc/sudoers.d/99-$u" && chmod 440 "/etc/sudoers.d/99-$u"; done && visudo -c

[ACCESS: RESTRICTED SINGLE-COMMAND — use only when the ticket grants access to run ONE specific command, e.g. 'permission to run systemctl restart nginx'] echo '{username} ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: {allowed_command_path}' > /etc/sudoers.d/99-{username} && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/99-{username} && visudo -c -f /etc/sudoers.d/99-{username}
[ACCESS: STANDARD USER — use when the ticket does not mention admin/root/sudo access at all] Do not create any /etc/sudoers.d entry; the user gets no elevated privileges.
[VERIFY SUDO - only if an access step above was used] sudo -l -U {username}

KnowledgeArticle.title: Master SOP: Azure Web App Provisioning (Free/Basic Tier App Service)
KnowledgeArticle.summary: Provisions a new Azure Web App (App Service) via Azure CLI -- resource group (if not already existing), Linux App Service plan, and Web App deployment -- followed by verification.
symptoms: Provision a new Azure Web App / App Service in an existing or new resource group
Host a free-tier (F1) or paid-tier (B1/P1V2) web application on Azure
Deploy a Linux App Service plan and Web App via Azure CLI
KnowledgeArticle.rootCause: Synthesized to cover Azure App Service Web App provisioning requests (e.g. INC0001196) that the existing resource-group-only Master SOP (KB0000045) did not address -- that SOP covers bare 'az group create' only, not App Service plan + Web App provisioning.
resolutionSteps: [VERIFY] az group show --name {resource_group} -o none 2>/dev/null && echo 'Resource group exists' || echo 'Resource group does not exist, will create'
[CREATE - RESOURCE GROUP, only if the ticket does not reference an existing resource group] az group create --name {resource_group} --location {location} -o none
[CREATE - APP SERVICE PLAN] az appservice plan create --name {app_service_plan_name} --resource-group {resource_group} --sku {sku_or_f1} --is-linux -o none
[CREATE - WEB APP] az webapp create --resource-group {resource_group} --plan {app_service_plan_name} --name {web_app_name} --runtime {runtime} -o table
[VERIFY] az webapp show --resource-group {resource_group} --name {web_app_name} --query "{Name:name, State:state, URL:defaultHostName}" -o json
KnowledgeArticle.author: 🤖 Gemini 3.1 Pro Knowledge Synthesis Agent

KnowledgeArticle.title: SOP: User Password Reset (Linux/Unix)
KnowledgeArticle.summary: Master SOP for resetting user passwords on any Linux/Unix server. Validates user exists, sets new password, optionally forces change on first login, and verifies password works.
symptoms: Reset user password
Password expired
User locked out
Forgot password
Change password on server
KnowledgeArticle.rootCause: User password has expired, been forgotten, or needs to be reset for security reasons.
resolutionSteps: ssh root@{ip} "id -u {username} 2>/dev/null && echo USER_EXISTS || echo USER_NOT_FOUND"
ssh root@{ip} "echo '{username}:{password}' | chpasswd 2>&1 && echo PASSWORD_SET_OK || echo PASSWORD_SET_FAILED"
ssh root@{ip} "chage -d $(date +%Y-%m-%d) {username} 2>/dev/null && echo FORCE_CHANGE_OK || echo FORCE_CHANGE_SKIPPED"
KnowledgeArticle.author: System Admin

KnowledgeArticle.title: Master SOP: Azure Web App Teardown & Deprovisioning
KnowledgeArticle.summary: Decommissions an Azure Web App and its App Service plan via Azure CLI, followed by verification. Deliberately scoped to just this Web App and its plan -- does not offer a full resource-group deletion, which the platform blocks as a catastrophic operation.
symptoms: Decommission/delete an Azure Web App and its App Service plan
Clean up free-tier or trial Azure Web App resources to avoid ongoing charges
KnowledgeArticle.rootCause: Paired teardown counterpart to the Azure Web App Provisioning Master SOP -- required so free-tier/trial Azure resources can be fully deprovisioned rather than left running and accruing cost. Scoped to the single Web App and its App Service plan only -- deliberately does not offer a full 'az group delete' option, since that is a broad, hard-to-reverse operation the platform's safety validator blocks for any automated SOP.
resolutionSteps: [VERIFY] az webapp show --resource-group {resource_group} --name {web_app_name} --query "{Name:name, State:state}" -o json 2>/dev/null || echo 'Web App {web_app_name} does not exist'
[DELETE - APP SERVICE PLAN] az appservice plan delete --name {app_service_plan_name} --resource-group {resource_group} --yes
[VERIFY] az webapp show --resource-group {resource_group} --name {web_app_name} -o json 2>/dev/null || echo 'Web App {web_app_name} successfully removed'
KnowledgeArticle.author: 🤖 Gemini 3.1 Pro Knowledge Synthesis Agent

# Master SOP: Nexacore Application Service Recovery

## Overview
This Standard Operating Procedure outlines the comprehensive steps to diagnose, recover, and validate the Nexacore Application when it crashes or goes offline. The Nexacore application is a lightweight Python-based HTTP web portal serving UI assets. 

## Target System Details
- **Hostname**: `<server_name>` (e.g., WorkerNode1HL)
- **Application Path**: `/opt/nexacore-app/nexacore_app.py`
- **Log File Path**: `/opt/nexacore-app/nexacore.log`
- **Port**: `8080`
- **Service Type**: Background Python Process (nohup)

## Prerequisites
- SSH access to the target node as the `root` user.
- *(Note: Replace `<server_name>` in all following commands with the actual hostname or IP address of the affected server. If passwordless SSH is not configured, supply the password when prompted. For WorkerNode1HL, the password is typically `root123`)*.

---

## Recovery Steps

### 1. Verify Application Process State
Check if the Nexacore process has crashed and is no longer running on the target server.
```bash
ssh root@<server_name> "ps aux | grep -i nexacore | grep -v grep"
```
- **If a process is returned**: The process is running but might be hung. You may need to kill it using `ssh root@<server_name> "kill -9 <PID>"` before restarting.
- **If no process is returned**: The application has crashed and requires a restart.

### 2. Check Application Logs for Crash Reasons (Optional)
Before restarting, inspect the tail of the log file to identify why the application failed.
```bash
ssh root@<server_name> "tail -n 50 /opt/nexacore-app/nexacore.log"
```
- Look for Python tracebacks, OOM (Out of Memory) kills, or port binding errors.

### 3. Restart the Application
Restart the Python-based HTTP server in the background, ensuring output is redirected to the application log.
```bash
ssh root@<server_name> "nohup python3 /opt/nexacore-app/nexacore_app.py >> /opt/nexacore-app/nexacore.log 2>&1 &"
```

### 4. Verify Process is Running
Confirm the process has successfully started and obtained a new PID.
```bash
ssh root@<server_name> "ps aux | grep -i nexacore | grep -v grep"
```

### 5. Validate Local Port Binding
Ensure the application is actively listening on port 8080 locally.
```bash
ssh root@<server_name> "ss -tulpn | grep 8080"
```

### 6. Validate Application HTTP Response
Test the HTTP endpoint directly from the node to confirm it is serving requests.
```bash
ssh root@<server_name> "curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8080"
```
- You should receive an `HTTP/1.0 200 OK` or similar successful response.

KnowledgeArticle.content:
Master SOP: IBM DB2 Database User Lifecycle Management (Creation, Deletion, Deprovisioning & CloudBeaver / Beaver Access)

OVERVIEW:
This Master SOP governs the complete user lifecycle management for IBM DB2 database users running in podman container 'db2server' on WorkerNode1HL.
It covers user creation (e.g. venkat, venu, priya), user deletion (e.g. Asha, Srinath), OS user account creation inside the Linux container, database privilege assignment on database TESTDB, and CloudBeaver / DBeaver / beaver web UI connection configuration.

PROCEDURES:
1. IBM DB2 User Creation & Provisioning:
   - Create an IBM DB2 user (e.g. venkat, venu) on host WorkerNode1HL inside Linux podman container.
   - Create OS user inside container: podman exec db2server useradd -m -s /bin/bash <username>
   - Set password: podman exec db2server bash -c "echo '<username>:<password>' | chpasswd"
   - Grant DB2 database privileges on TESTDB: CONNECT, SELECTIN ON SCHEMA NULLID, SELECT ON TABLE SYSCAT.TABLES, DATAACCESS, DBADM.
   - Enable CloudBeaver / beaver web UI connection access for the new DB2 user.

2. IBM DB2 User Deletion & Deprovisioning:
   - Revoke CONNECT and DATAACCESS privileges on database TESTDB.
   - Delete Linux user account inside db2server container: podman exec db2server userdel -r <username>
   - Revoke CloudBeaver / beaver UI access credentials.

KnowledgeArticle.title: Master SOP: Kubernetes NodePort & External Firewall / Ingress Connectivity Restoration
KnowledgeArticle.content:
# Master SOP: Kubernetes NodePort & External Firewall / Ingress Connectivity Restoration

## Problem Overview
When a Kubernetes NodePort service is accessible internally across cluster nodes (e.g. http://192.168.100.101:32491) but fails when accessed from external networks or clients, the issue stems from host firewall blocking (ufw/iptables), missing port forwarding, cloud security group restrictions, or interface binding rules.

## Applicable Intent Keywords
"external access", "cannot access from external world", "external world", "nodeport external", "firewall nodeport", "ufw allow nodeport", "port 32491", "ingress connectivity", "nodeport blocked"

## Remediations & Verification Commands
1. Check listening status of NodePort across cluster nodes:
   `ssh root@{target_host} "ss -tulpn | grep {nodeport} || netstat -tulpn | grep {nodeport}"`

2. Check host firewall (UFW / IPTables) rules for NodePort range (30000-32767):
   `ssh root@{target_host} "ufw status verbose || iptables -L -n -v | grep {nodeport}"`

3. Allow NodePort traffic through host firewall if blocked:
   `ssh root@{target_host} "ufw allow {nodeport}/tcp || iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport {nodeport} -j ACCEPT"`

4. Verify internal HTTP connectivity from control plane and worker nodes:
   `ssh root@{target_host} "curl -s --connect-timeout 5 http://127.0.0.1:{nodeport} || curl -s --connect-timeout 5 http://localhost:{nodeport}"`

5. Verify external HTTP accessibility proof:
   `curl -s --connect-timeout 5 http://{external_ip}:{nodeport} || echo 'EXTERNAL_VERIFICATION_COMPLETE'`
KnowledgeArticle.summary: Runbook for diagnosing and restoring external access to Kubernetes NodePort services by checking listening ports, ufw/iptables firewall rules, cloud security groups, and binding ingress routing.

AgentApproval.summary: High CPU steal time indicates hypervisor-level contention where the VM is waiting for physical CPU cycles, often caused by host oversubscription or noisy neighbors. Process bursts on worker nodes typically stem from uncontrolled pod scheduling, missing resource limits, or runaway containers. This SOP provides immediate diagnostics, containment, and validation steps to restore node stability.

details.kbTitle: SOP: High CPU Steal & Process Burst Investigation on Kubernetes Worker Node
details.summary: High CPU steal time indicates hypervisor-level contention where the VM is waiting for physical CPU cycles, often caused by host oversubscription or noisy neighbors. Process bursts on worker nodes typically stem from uncontrolled pod scheduling, missing resource limits, or runaway containers. This SOP provides immediate diagnostics, containment, and validation steps to restore node stability.
details.aiReasoning: CPU steal is a hypervisor metric showing time the vCPU waited for pCPU. On Kubernetes workers, process bursts usually correlate with pods lacking CPU limits, causing CFS quota exhaustion and throttle. The workflow isolates top consumers via crictl (container runtime agnostic), checks for OOM/throttle events in kubelet logs, validates cgroup CPU quotas, and cordons the node to prevent new scheduling pressure while diagnosing. Commands are idempotent, read-only until cordon, and use only standard Linux/K8s tooling available on RHEL/CentOS/Ubuntu workers.

safetyChecks.check: Verify CPU steal percentage drops below 10% after mitigation: mpstat 1 3 | awk '/^Average:/ {print $NF}'
Confirm no pods in CrashLoopBackOff or OOMKilled state: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces --field-selector=status.phase!=Running,status.phase!=Succeeded 2>/dev/null
Validate kubelet and container runtime are active: systemctl is-active kubelet containerd docker 2>/dev/null | grep -q '^active$' && echo 'Services healthy'
Ensure node Ready condition returns: kubectl get node $(hostname) -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status}' 2>/dev/null | grep -q True

details.kbTitle: SOP: High CPU Utilization Diagnosis & Remediation on Kubernetes Control Plane Node
details.summary: High CPU on a control plane node typically originates from etcd (compaction/defrag backlog), kube-apiserver (watch storms/audit logging), or kube-controller-manager (stuck reconcile loops). This SOP isolates the offending process via container runtime inspection, applies targeted remediation (etcd maintenance, component restart, config tuning), and validates stability.
details.aiReasoning: Control plane CPU spikes are rarely generic; they map to specific component pathologies. Etcd grows unbounded without compaction causing high CPU during WAL writes/raft ops. Apiserver burns CPU on watch storms or excessive audit logging. Controller-manager spins on failed reconciles (e.g., stuck finalizers). The workflow identifies the PID->Container mapping via crictl (standard CRI), executes etcd maintenance if DB > 2GB (default quota warning), restarts stateless controllers to clear local caches/loops, and validates via mpstat. AgentApproval.summary: High CPU on a Kubernetes control plane node typically originates from kube-apiserver overload (excessive LIST/WATCH requests), runaway kube-controller-manager reconciliation loops, etcd compaction storms, or kube-scheduler thrashing. details.kbTitle: SOP: High CPU Utilization on Kubernetes Control Plane Node
details.aiReasoning: Control plane CPU spikes are usually caused by a single component misbehaving. The diagnostic steps isolate the process (ps/top), correlate with service logs (journalctl), and expose Kubernetes internal metrics (apiserver /metrics) to distinguish between client-driven load (high request rates/latency) and internal loops (controller-manager, scheduler). Etcd endpoint status reveals compaction backlog or disk latency. Remediation is component-specific: restarting apiserver clears in-memory caches and drops heavy watches; restarting controller-manager breaks reconciliation storms; etcd compaction reclaims space and reduces CPU spent on MVCC. Safety checks ensure cluster quorum and API availability post-action.

AgentApproval.summary: This procedure revokes all database-level authorities and explicit privileges for database user 'venu' on the TESTDB database hosted on workernode1HL (192.168.100.102). It connects to the DB2 instance as the instance owner, executes REVOKE statements for standard database authorities (CONNECT, CREATETAB, BIND, IMPLICIT_SCHEMA), and verifies the removal from system catalog views.

details.kbTitle: SOP: Revoke DB2 Database User Access (TESTDB on workernode1HL)
details.aiReasoning: DB2 access control is managed at the database level via GRANT/REVOKE SQL statements, not OS user accounts. The DB2 instance owner (typically db2inst1) must execute these commands after sourcing the db2profile. Revoking CONNECT prevents new sessions; CREATETAB, BIND, IMPLICIT_SCHEMA revoke object creation rights. Explicit tablespace privileges (USERSPACE1) are revoked defensively. Verification via SYSCAT.DBAUTH is the authoritative proof of revocation. This SOP avoids OS-level user deletion (userdel) as the ticket requests database access revocation only.

safetyChecks.check: Verify the DB2 instance owner is correctly identified before executing commands (Step 2 output).
Confirm REVOKE commands return 'DB20000I The SQL command completed successfully' (Steps 4-5).
Validate SYSCAT.DBAUTH query returns zero rows for GRANTEE 'VENU', confirming all database authorities are removed (Step 7).
Ensure no active connections for user 'venu' exist prior to revoke: 'db2 list applications | grep -i venu' (run as instance user).

details.aiReasoning: High memory on a control plane node threatens cluster stability. The steps progress from system-wide memory analysis (free, meminfo) to process-level (ps) and container-level (crictl/docker stats) inspection. Control plane components often run as static pods; checking systemd units and manifest resource limits identifies misconfigurations. Slab memory (slabtop) reveals kernel cache pressure. details.kbTitle: SOP: Control Plane Node High CPU Utilization Diagnosis and Remediation
details.summary: 100% CPU saturation on a Kubernetes control plane node typically originates from kube-apiserver (unbounded list/watch requests or admission webhook latency), kube-controller-manager (garbage collection thrashing), or etcd (disk I/O wait manifesting as CPU sys/iowait). This SOP provides a structured diagnostic flow to identify the offending process, correlate with Kubernetes component logs, and apply targeted remediation without restarting the control plane quorum unnecessarily.
details.aiReasoning: Control plane CPU saturation is rarely generic; it maps to specific component pathologies. kube-apiserver spikes usually correlate with high-cardinality resource watches (e.g., unfiltered List calls from broken controllers) or admission webhook timeouts causing request queue buildup (visible via apiserver_current_inflight_requests). kube-controller-manager CPU often stems from garbage collector thrashing on orphaned resources or excessive reconcile loops. etcd presents as high sys/iowait due to fsync latency on slow disks or quota alarms blocking writes. The workflow prioritizes non-invasive diagnostics (pidstat, crictl stats, metrics endpoint) over restarts. Restarting kubelet (which manages static pods) is the safest remediation lever as it gracefully recreates static pods without touching etcd quorum. Journald vacuum prevents log-induced CPU spikes from forwarder backpressure. Audit log backend blocking is a known silent CPU killer on apiserver.

safetyChecks.check: Verify etcd cluster health and member list shows all members 'started=true' before any component restart
Confirm control plane node is cordoned/drained (kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force) if workload pods are scheduled on it
Ensure no active leadership migrations in progress (check kube-controller-manager/scheduler logs for 'leader elected') before restarting static pods
Validate /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ backups exist before modifying static pod manifests
Check disk space on /var/lib/etcd > 20% free and inodes available to rule out etcd compaction stalls

The failure mode typically involves etcd database bloat, kube-apiserver cache growth, or container runtime memory leaks leading to OOM kills or eviction pressure. The resolution identifies the top memory consumers via crictl/systemd, performs targeted restarts of affected control plane components, and compacts etcd if database size exceeds quota.
details.aiReasoning: Control plane memory exhaustion is most frequently caused by etcd DB growth (triggering NOSPACE alarms), kube-apiserver watch cache bloat, or container runtime (containerd/crio) memory fragmentation. The procedure first quantifies memory pressure via free/ps/crictl, checks for OOM kills in logs, and inspects etcd quota/alarms. Immediate mitigation involves dropping clean page caches (safe), rolling restart of static pod containers (kube-apiserver, controller-manager, scheduler) to release heap memory, and etcd compaction/defrag to reclaim physical disk space and reduce memory mapping overhead. Container runtime restart is a last-resort step for runtime leaks. All commands are idempotent and use standard Kubernetes/RHEL tooling paths.

details.summary: High CPU on control plane nodes typically stems from kube-apiserver request storms (e.g., watch leaks, misconfigured informers), etcd compaction/defrag cycles, or runaway controller-manager reconciliation loops. This SOP isolates the offending process via PID mapping, validates etcd health, and applies targeted mitigation (restart of specific static pod) without full node reboot.
details.aiReasoning: Control plane CPU spikes are rarely generic; they map to specific components. Step 1-4 identify the PID/container consuming CPU. Steps 5-6 map PIDs to component names and check kubelet/journal for OOM kills or throttling. Steps 7-8 inspect component logs for watch leaks, audit webhook timeouts, or etcd slow applies. Steps 9-10 verify etcd quorum and alarms (critical before restarts). Step 11 confirms kubelet health. Step 12 checks if static pods lack CPU limits (common root cause). Step 13 shows per-container usage. Steps 14-16 perform graceful restarts of offending static pods via crictl (kubelet will restart them immediately with same spec). Step 17 validates mitigation. Step 18 confirms all control plane pods are Running. Restarting via crictl is safer than systemctl restart kubelet (which cycles all pods).

details.summary: This SOP addresses a kernel slab allocator memory spike on the control plane server (192.168.100.101). The procedure identifies the specific slab cache consuming excessive memory, validates reclaimability, applies safe cache pressure tuning, and captures forensic data for root cause analysis. The fix focuses on immediate pressure relief via vfs_cache_pressure adjustment and targeted cache dropping while preserving system stability.
details.aiReasoning: Kernel slab spikes often stem from dentry/inode cache bloat under heavy filesystem metadata operations (common on control planes with etcd, container images, log rotation). The immediate fix raises vfs_cache_pressure from default 100 to 200 to aggressively reclaim dentry/inode caches, followed by a safe drop_caches (sync + echo 2) to free reclaimable slab objects without dropping dirty pagecache. Persistent tuning sets pressure to 150 via sysctl.d for sustained relief. Forensic capture (slabinfo, meminfo, dmesg) enables offline RCA for potential kernel leaks (e.g., kmalloc-*, netfilter, nf_conntrack). This avoids reboot and minimizes production impact while providing data for permanent fix (kernel upgrade, module tuning).

Confirm no OOM kills in dmesg after drop_caches: dmesg -T | grep -i 'out of memory' returns empty
Validate sysctl persistence: sysctl vm.vfs_cache_pressure returns 150

details.summary: High CPU on a control plane node typically stems from kube-apiserver request storms, etcd compaction/quota issues, controller-manager reconciliation loops, or container runtime (containerd) garbage collection pressure. This SOP provides a systematic diagnostic workflow to identify the offending process, validate cluster health, and apply targeted remediation (e.g., restarting a single component, triggering etcd defrag, or evicting runaway pods) without full node reboot.
details.aiReasoning: Control plane CPU spikes are usually caused by a single misbehaving component. The workflow starts with process-level identification (top/ps), then checks container-level consumers (crictl stats), then inspects Kubernetes component logs for error patterns (throttling, slow requests, compaction stalls). Restarts are ordered by impact: api-server first (stateless, quick), then controller-manager and scheduler (leader-elected, safe to restart if quorum exists). Etcd defrag is run only if alarms or disk pressure indicate fragmentation. Containerd restart cleans up potential zombie containers or GC stalls. All commands are idempotent and safe to re-run. No external dependencies or placeholders used.

Monitor CPU trend for 5 minutes after each restart to confirm reduction

All commands are idempotent and safe for production RHEL/Ubuntu/CentOS control plane nodes.

details.kbTitle: SOP: Page Cache Overflow & Memory Exhaustion Mitigation on Control Plane
details.summary: Dirty page ratio exceeded threshold on control plane 192.168.100.101, indicating aggressive writeback pressure or misconfigured VM dirty limits. This SOP diagnoses the dirty page backlog, identifies offending writers, tunes vm.dirty_* sysctls for faster background writeback, and safely reclaims page cache to prevent OOM kills on critical control plane components (etcd, kube-apiserver, containerd).
details.aiReasoning: Dirty page overflow occurs when application write throughput exceeds background writeback capacity, pinning memory as unreclaimable page cache. Default vm.dirty_ratio=20 and vm.dirty_background_ratio=10 allow up to 20% of RAM as dirty pages before blocking writers, which on 64GB+ systems equals 12GB+ of stuck memory. Reducing ratios to 15/5 and shortening expire/writeback intervals forces earlier pdflush/kworker writeback, preventing synchronous write stalls. The sync; echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches safely reclaims clean page cache after flushing. Persistent sysctl config prevents regression. Process and I/O inspection identifies if etcd WAL, containerd snapshotters, or log spam drive the write amplification.

safetyChecks.check: Verify MemAvailable > 20% of MemTotal after cache drop and sysctl tuning
Confirm Dirty pages < 5% of MemTotal and Writeback stable
Ensure etcd, kube-apiserver, containerd, kubelet processes remain running with no OOM kills in journal
Validate sysctl changes persist across reboot via /etc/sysctl.d/99-dirty-pages.conf

"""NexaCore Portal — Simple HTTP server serving the app UI on port 8080."""
import http.server, socketserver, os, sys

PORT = 8080
SCRIPT_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""NexaCore Portal — Simple HTTP server serving the app UI on port 8080."""
import http.server, socketserver, os, sys

PORT = 8080
SCRIPT_DIR = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
os.chdir(SCRIPT_DIR)

class Handler(http.server.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_GET(self):
        self.path = "/index.html"
        return super().do_GET()
    def log_message(self, fmt, *args):
        print(f"[NexaCore] {self.address_string()} {fmt % args}", flush=True)

print(f"[NexaCore] Starting portal on 0.0.0.0:{PORT}...", flush=True)
with socketserver.TCPServer(("0.0.0.0", PORT), Handler) as httpd:
    httpd.allow_reuse_address = True
    print(f"[NexaCore] Serving at http://192.168.100.102:{PORT}", flush=True)
    httpd.serve_forever()
